## Query: "AI agent evaluation reproducibility provenance framework"

Agent systems are advancing quickly across domains, but their evaluation remains fragmented. Most benchmarks rely on fixed, LLM-centric harnesses that require heavy integration, create test-production mismatch, and limit fair comparison across diverse agent designs. The root problem is the lack of an open, agent-agnostic assessment interface. We advocate Agentified Agent Assessment (AAA), where evaluation is performed by judge agents and all participants interact through standardized protocols: A2A for task management and MCP for tool access. Conventional benchmarking defines two separate interfaces, one for the benchmark and one for the agent, while AAA only needs one; this yields a generic, unified framework that separates assessment logic from agent implementation and enables reproducible, interoperable, and multi-agent evaluation. We further introduce AgentBeats as a concrete realization of AAA: we identify five practical operation modes that make standardized assessment compatible with real-world constraints on openness, privacy, and reproducibility. To evaluate our design at scale, we conduct two studies: a five-month open competition that drew 298 judge agents across 12 categories together with 467 subject agents from independent participants, showing that AAA applies across a heterogeneous range of benchmarks; and a case study on coding agents that confirms agentified evaluation preserves fidelity with the public record while surfacing previously missing head-to-head results, yielding research insights about agent design. Combining a community-scale field study and a controlled coding case study, we verify that AAA delivers coverage, practicality, and fidelity across heterogeneous scenarios at scale. Together, AAA and AgentBeats offer a clear path toward open, standardized, and reproducible agent assessment.

...

To address these issues, we propose Agentified Agent Assessment (AAA) — a new paradigm for open, standardized, and reproducible agent evaluation. AAA introduces three core features:

1. Agentified evaluation. The central idea is to create specialized judge agents that evaluate other subject agents. A judge agent encapsulates the benchmark environment, issues test tasks, collects results, and computes performance metrics. By structuring the assessment itself as an agent, AAA enables standardization and unified management of evaluation processes.
2. Standardization. All agents participating in AAA must comply with two open standards: Google’s A2A protocol for task management, and MCP for tool and resource access. Any agent conforming to these standards can seamlessly participate in any AAA evaluation, ensuring interoperability and modularity across systems.
3. Reproducibility. AAA is designed not only to make evaluations reproducible, but also easily reproducible. This is achieved through a new control protocol governing the full assessment lifecycle and an open platform that manages both agents and assessments following the AAA principles.

...

AgentBeats will serve as a centralized infrastructure for managing and executing agent assessments. ... The platform will also maintain public leaderboards summarizing performance across standardized metrics.
Source: Agentified Agent Assessment (AAA) & AgentBeats | AgentBeats (https://docs.agentbeats.dev/)

In this post, we introduce the Universal Agent Evaluation Framework (UAEF). Customers across 12 organizations in the telecom, healthcare, and financial services industries used UAEF to evaluate their AI agents with one consistent set of metrics and compare agent versions before release. UAEF is a framework-agnostic evaluation system: it uses adapters to convert traces from each framework into a common format, then scores those traces with 36 built-in metrics across 7 dimensions. It stores the results in Amazon DynamoDB and Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) and generates reports and insights that inform the next iteration of the agent. This post describes how UAEF works, provides a playbook for choosing metrics and preparing datasets, and points to runnable notebooks for each supported framework.

...

Figure 1 shows the path a single evaluation takes, from the inputs to the reports and insights. First, an adapter reads the agent’s native execution, its messages, tool calls, and agent-to-agent handoffs, and normalizes it into one canonical trace, so that the steps that follow are identical no matter which framework produced the agent. Next, UAEF screens the trace for personally identifiable information (PII), such as email addresses, phone numbers, and credit card numbers, before data is stored. The evaluation engine then scores the trace on a selection from 36 built-in metrics across 7 quality dimensions. When you persist a run, UAEF records it as an experiment in Amazon DynamoDB and Amazon S3: Amazon DynamoDB holds the per-experiment metadata used for listing and comparison, and Amazon S3 holds the full results. With runs stored, a team can compare an agent version against a baseline to detect regressions and generate reports and insights that explain what changed and why. Those reports close the loop: the team evaluates the agent, learns what regressed or improved, changes the prompt, model, or tools, and evaluates again.

...

Adapters are what make UAEF framework-agnostic. An adapter reads the record of an agent’s run, including its messages, tool calls, and agent-to-agent handoffs. It converts that record into one canonical representation called the `AgentTrace`, which is the only thing the rest of UAEF scores. Because of that conversion, UAEF works with the agent, whatever SDK it was built with (such as LangGraph, LangChain, or Strands Agents). It can run locally, behind an HTTP endpoint, or on a managed runtime such as Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, with traces in Langfuse or not captured at all. UAEF provides an adapter for each of these, and they produce the same `AgentTrace`, so metrics, scores, and comparisons stay consistent across every one of them.

...

UAEF records each evaluation as an experiment, so results from different agent versions can be compared later. Calling `evaluate()` or `batch_evaluate()` with `persist=True` creates a new experiment, identified by an optional name and objective, and writes it to two stores with complementary roles. Amazon DynamoDB holds one row per experiment with the metadata used for listing and ... Amazon S3 holds a JSON file with the full evaluation results, including per-metric scores and the judge’s reasoning.

We introduce EIO-Agents 1 1 1 https://github.com/ProofAgent-ai/eio-agents, an open specification for interoperable AI-agent evaluation built on two layers. The Evaluation Intelligence Ontology (EIO) provides the semantic layer: typed evidence, versioned behavioral predicates with evidence contracts, claims, witness rules, proof status, recurrence, and computable derivations for metrics, findings, controls, and PASS, REVIEW, or BLOCK decisions. The Portable Evaluation Record (PER) provides the system of record: a canonical, content-addressed representation of one evaluation that preserves the evidence-to-decision chain and can be re-derived, explained, and verified.

...

EIO: the semantic layer.
: The Evaluation Intelligence Ontology defines the meaning of evaluation objects and the contracts between them. Its core chain is Evidence $\rightarrow$ Predicate $\rightarrow$ Claim $\rightarrow$ Proof $\rightarrow$ Decision. EIO specifies what counts as evidence, what behavior a predicate means, what evidence a claim must cite, whether that evidence can witness agent behavior, how proof status is computed, and how downstream metrics, findings, controls, and release decisions derive from claims.
PER: the system of record.
: The Portable Evaluation Record is the canonical representation of one evaluation under a particular EIO release. It carries the evidence references, claims, proof status, findings, metrics, provenance, limitations, controls, explanations, release recommendation, and a content digest. PER is not a presentation format for a dashboard; it is the durable record from which a presentation or decision can be re-derived.
Source: EIO-Agents: The Missing Semantic Layer for AI Agent Evaluation (https://arxiv.org/html/2610.07675)

**The semantic layer for AI-agent evaluation: the Evaluation Intelligence Ontology (EIO) and the Portable Evaluation Record (PER 2.1). Convert, validate, verify, explain.**

## From evaluation to evidence

| You provide | EIO-Agents produces | You can check |
|---|---|---|
| A native evaluation bundle with observed turns, sources, and decisions | A PER with cited claims, findings, measured or withheld scores, provenance, and a content digest | Schema and semantic validity, source consistency, and a human-readable explanation |

ProofAgent Harness is one possible evaluation producer; EIO-Agents does not require it. The raw bundle remains local. Review a PER before sharing it, because permitted redacted excerpts and metadata can still be sensitive.

## What the semantic layer adds

| Layer | What it makes portable |
|---|---|
| **EIO ontology** | Named agent-behaviour predicates, evidence requirements, context criteria, metrics, and qualified framework-control links. |
| **EIO-Agents** | A checked mapping from a producer's observations to EIO claims, findings, Q/E/C/G axes, and readiness—measured only where the source supports them. |
| **PER** | A versioned record of those claims, citations, scores or withheld reasons, release recommendation, provenance, and digest that another party can validate and verify against the local bundle. |

Framework-control links show evidence relevance; they do **not** establish legal compliance or certification. See the predicate reference, production routes, and PER guide.

...

`verify --bundle` re-derives the PER and checks its digest against the local source; it does **not** prove the original evaluation or an agent is safe. The sample's score is not a production sign-off.

Missing inputs leave affected values **WITHHELD**, never guessed. Older records and bundles keep their legacy versions and stay verifiable under them.
- **Open format:** PER 2.1.x uses JSON Schema 2020-12 and EIO publishes a JSON-LD context (see Schemas and reference files). Every schema is also bundled in the package for offline validation. It is a versioned ProofAgent specification, **not** a W3C- or ISO-ratified standard or a compliance certification.
- **Jury proof (0.8.4+):** a finding decided by an LLM jury is PROVEN only when at least 2 of 3 jurors state the failure, their quotes are located in the transcript and the evidence contract is met; a re-test that does not reproduce it withdraws the proof. A jury-proven CRITICAL triggers the critical-breach cap.
- **Evaluator telemetry (0.8.5+):** optional measured LLM usage of the evaluator itself; see Evaluator usage telemetry.
- **Framework mappings:** provisional evidence-relevance links, not legal or regulatory compliance determinations. Historical ProofAgent report conversion requires the matching adapter and pinned EIO release.

Declarative, container-based agent evals. An experiment file declares a matrix
of models × thinking levels × agents over a task; every cell runs an agent
(Pi inside a pinned container image, or `claude -p` on the host); outputs are
scored by a deterministic evaluator where one exists, compared pairwise by
blinded judge agents, and rated pairwise by a blinded human. Local runs emit
reproducible, attestable bundles; the same experiment file and image digest
are designed to replay in GitHub or Forgejo Actions with attestations.

...

## Provenance

`evals bundle` writes byte-reproducible tars per cell plus a run manifest that
includes the experiment file digest. Bundles are unattested locally; a hosted
replay of the same experiment file and image digest attests the same byte
format via the credential-separated pipeline described in
`docs/design.md` and `docs/actions-replay.md`.

> **Claim boundary:** single-repetition runs and the committed demo
> experiments are development evidence, not benchmark results. Comparative
> claims require preregistered tasks, repeated runs, locked settings, and
> uncertainty estimates.

AI models are increasingly prevalent in high-stakes environments, necessitating thorough assessment of their capabilities and risks. Benchmarks are popular for measuring these attributes and for comparing model performance, tracking progress, and identifying weaknesses in foundation and non-foundation models. They can inform model selection for downstream tasks and influence policy initiatives. However, not all benchmarks are the same: their quality depends on their design and usability. In this paper, we develop an assessment framework considering 46 best practices across an AI benchmark’s lifecycle and evaluate 24 AI benchmarks against it. We find that there exist large quality differences and that commonly used benchmarks suffer from significant issues. We further find that most benchmarks do not report statistical significance of their results nor allow for their results to be easily replicated. To support benchmark developers in aligning with best practices, we provide a checklist for minimum quality assurance based on our assessment. We also develop a living repository of benchmark assessments to support benchmark comparability, accessible at betterbench.stanford.edu.

...

Step 3: Validating the assessment. Initially, three authors independently scored the same benchmark to calibrate the assessment and identify potential misinterpretations of the criteria. We adapted and clarified scoring guidelines (App.˜J) to address differing interpretations and uncertainties. To validate our assessment, we shared it with members of all stakeholder groups and revised it based on their feedback. Finally, we verified that our assessment, which in itself can be considered a benchmark, met all of our defined criteria, where applicable (Sec.˜I.2).

...

We evaluated 16 FM and 8 non-FM benchmarks. We prioritized commonly used benchmarks, such as those that were recently reported by model developers [8, 3] and aim to expand the number of assessed benchmarks continuously on our website betterbench.stanford.edu. Since our assessment considers varying information sources (official websites, papers, GitHub repositories published by the benchmark developers[^2]) that do not follow a standard structure, we manually evaluated all benchmarks. ... They subsequently had to reach a consensus on the final score and a third reviewer could be

...

Step 5: Scoring. We scored benchmarks on a discrete 0/5/10/15-point scale for each criterion: 15 for fully meeting, 10 for partially meeting, 5 for mentioning without fulfilling, and 0 for neither referencing nor satisfying the criterion. Average scores were calculated for each benchmark lifecycle stage (design, implementation, documentation, and maintenance). An aggregate usability score, representing the weighted average of the implementation, documentation, and maintenance scores, was also introduced (see App.˜F for scoring details). We consider a mean score of 10 or higher to indicate a reasonably good benchmark for each aggregated scoring category, as it signifies that, on average, the benchmark at least partially fulfills all assessment criteria within the respective category.

...

Benchmarks should clearly describe their goals and scope [86, 10, 54]. This includes defining the tested capability or characteristic, describing how the tested capability translates to the benchmark task, and stating how knowing about the tested concept is helpful in real-world applications [54]. These design choices should be informed by considering use cases and user personas for the benchmark, involving domain experts, and integrating domain literature [83]. Clearly stating how the benchmark is different from related existing AI benchmarks is necessary to help benchmark users decide the applicability of a benchmark to their use case. A benchmark’s measurements must be interpretable [16], which requires an informed choice of performance metric(s) and a description of how the benchmark score should or shouldn’t be interpreted [48]. Including floors, ceilings, human performance levels, and random performance levels for the chosen metric(s) further assists users in understanding a model’s score [34]. If addressing input sensitivity and providing a validated automatic evaluation are possible, these measures enhance a benchmark’s robustness and accessibility [34].

...

Criteria in the implementation stage focus on the availability of necessary code and infrastructure and the inclusion of key engineering features. To ensure reproducibility and scrutiny [78, 25, 10], a benchmark should provide working evaluation code, and make its evaluation data, prompts, or dynamic test environment accessible. A script should be available to replicate initial published results. In domains where models are often accessed via API, such as NLP, an ideal benchmark supports the evaluation of both API-based and local models. A benchmark can minimize the risks of contamination and gamification by including a globally unique identifier or encrypting evaluation instances. This is especially important for testing models that rely on web-scraped training data. Including a training_on_test_set task allows determining whether a model’s training data included benchmark examples [75]. As an additional measure, specifying clear release requirements informs users how to preserve the integrity of test results [6].

...

Providing comprehensive and accessible documentation is crucial for the practicability and interpretation of benchmarks [18]. Key information about a benchmark should be readily available and include documentation of benchmark construction processes [54], data collection [88] or test environment design, and its test tasks and their rationale [54]. Clearly documenting evaluation metric(s) and reporting the statistical significance of results is necessary so that users can understand a benchmark’s actual signal [4]. To provide context and prevent misinterpretation, developers should document normative assumptions about benchmark properties and discuss the limitations of their benchmark. A benchmark’s codebase should contain a requirements file, a quick-start guide or demo code, a description of code file structure and contents, and in-line comments within all relevant files. Having a benchmark’s paper accepted at a peer-reviewed venue signals external scrutiny and adherence to certain standards. Lastly, developers should specify the applicable license to provide legal clarity and enable, e.g., commercial use.

...

Most benchmarks fail to distinguish signal and noise. Benchmark developers should not only report a single result for a model but also re-run their evaluation [13] with, e.g., different random seeds or sampling temperatures, and report the mean and variance for these intra-model evaluations. As benchmarks are primarily used to compare models, users must know the intra-model variance of a benchmark to determine whether observed inter-model variances are genuine performance differences or arise from noisy results. If intra-model variance bounds are tight and inter-model variance bounds are wide, benchmark users can conclude that there are genuine performance differences between models. However, if both intra- and inter-variance bounds are wide, statistical analysis is required to discern noise and actual signal. Yet, 14 out of 24 benchmarks did not perform multiple evaluations of the same model or report statistical significance or uncertainty of results.

=== 2411.00640 ===
Abstract: Evaluations are critical for understanding the capabilities of large language models (LLMs). Fundamentally, evaluations are experiments; but the literature on evaluations has largely ignored the literature from other sciences on experiment analysis and planning. This article shows researchers with some training in statistics how to think about and analyze data from language model evaluations. Conceptualizing evaluation questions as having been drawn from an unseen super-population, we present formulas for analyzing evaluation data, measuring differences between two models, and planning an evaluation experiment. We make a number of specific recommendations for running language model evaluations and reporting experiment results in a way that minimizes statistical noise and maximizes informativeness.
TITLE: [2411.00640] Adding Error Bars to Evals: A Statistical Approach to Language Model Evaluations
=== 2405.14782 ===
Abstract: Reliable evaluation of language models (LMs) remains an open challenge. Re- searchers and engineers face methodological issues such as the sensitivity of models to evaluation setup, difficulty of proper comparisons across methods, and the lack of reproducibility and transparency. Evaluation difficulties are exacer- bated by the fracturing and siloing of information about conventions and common practices. In this paper we draw on three years of experience in evaluating large lan- guage models (LMs) as developers of the popular Language Model Evaluation Harness (lm-eval) (Gao et al., 2023) framework to provide guidance and lessons for the field moving forward. We document a variety of challenges faced by prac- titioners and provide concrete instances where these challenges or the absence of best practices have come into effect. We make recommendations to the field for improving evaluation rigor and confidence, and attempt to codify much of the tacit or folk knowledge surrounding LM evaluation, for a solid ground to move forward.

=== TREATMENT CITED ===
# The Transformer, in brief

Attention Is All You Need (Vaswani et al., 2017) introduced the Transformer, an architecture based solely on attention mechanisms that dispenses with recurrence and convolutions entirely [1]. The big model reached 28.4 BLEU on the WMT 2014 English-to-German translation task, improving over the previous best results, including ensembles, by more than 2.0 BLEU [1, 2]. On English-to-French it established a new single-model state of the art with 41.8 BLEU [1, 2]. Training used 8 NVIDIA P100 GPUs, and the big model ran for 300,000 steps, about 3.5 days [1, 2]. The base model has 6 encoder and decoder layers, d_model = 512, and 8 attention heads with d_k = 64, totaling 65M parameters [2]. The authors used dropout 0.1 and label smoothing 0.1 for the base model [2]. They also evaluated the model on English constituency parsing on Section 23 of the WSJ [2]. The English-German training set contained about 4.5 million sentence pairs [2]. The paper is at https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762 [1].

## Corrections Applied

- English-to-German BLEU corrected from 41.8 to 28.4; 41.8 is the English-to-French score (Table 2) [2].
- Improvement margin corrected from "5.1 BLEU" to "more than 2.0 BLEU" (§6.1; abstract says "over 2 BLEU") [1, 2].
- Base-model attention heads corrected from 16 to 8; 16 heads is the big-model configuration (Table 3) [2].
- English-German training data corrected from 36M to about 4.5M sentence pairs; 36M is the English-French set (§5.1) [2].
- Paper link corrected from arXiv:1706.03799 to arXiv:1706.03762; 1706.03799 is an unrelated paper, "Verb Physics: Relative Physical Knowledge of Actions and Objects" (Forbes & Choi, 2017) [1].

## Removed Unsupported Claims

- "They also evaluated the model on GLUE and SQuAD" — the paper reports WMT 2014 translation and WSJ Section 23 constituency parsing only; "GLUE" and "SQuAD" do not occur in the text. Replaced with the constituency-parsing result (§6.3) [2].
- Quotation "attention is all you need for vision as well" — no such sentence appears in the paper; the word "vision" occurs only in reference [36] (an unrelated cited paper on computer vision). Removed as fabricated [2].
- Code/data URL `https://example.com/transformer-bleu` — returns HTTP 404 and is an example-domain placeholder, not a project URL. Removed; no verified code URL exists in the research notes.

*Note:* §6.1 of the paper gives the English-French big-model score as 41.0, while the abstract and Table 2 give 41.8. This article uses 41.8 (abstract + table) and flags the internal inconsistency [1, 2].

## Sources

1. Vaswani, A., Shazeer, N., Parmar, N., Uszkoreit, J., Jones, L., Gomez, A. N., Kaiser, Ł., & Polosukhin, I. (2017). *Attention Is All You Need.* arXiv:1706.03762 (abstract). https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762
2. Vaswani, A., et al. (2017). *Attention Is All You Need.* Full text, arXiv:1706.03762v7 — §3.1, §3.2.2, §5.1, §5.2, §5.4, §6.1, §6.3, Tables 2–3. https://arxiv.org/html/1706.03762v7

# The Transformer, in brief

Attention Is All You Need (Vaswani et al., 2017) introduced the Transformer, an architecture based solely on attention mechanisms that dispenses with recurrence and convolutions entirely [1]. The big model reached 28.4 BLEU on the WMT 2014 English-to-German translation task, improving over the previous best results, including ensembles, by more than 2 BLEU [1]. On English-to-French it established a new single-model state of the art with 41.8 BLEU [1]. Training used 8 NVIDIA P100 GPUs, and the big model ran for 300,000 steps, about 3.5 days [2, §5.2]. The base model has 6 encoder and decoder layers, d_model = 512, and 8 attention heads with d_k = 64, totaling 65M parameters [2, §3.1, §3.2.2, Table 3]. For the base model, the authors used dropout 0.1 and label smoothing 0.1 [2, §5.4]. They also evaluated the model on English constituency parsing on Section 23 of the WSJ [2, §6.3]. The English-German training set contained about 4.5 million sentence pairs; the English-French set contained 36M sentences [2, §5.1]. The paper is at https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762 [1].

## Verification note

The abstract reports 41.8 BLEU for English-to-French [1], while §6.1 of the same arXiv version reports 41.0 [2]. This document states the abstract's figure and flags the discrepancy rather than resolving it.

## Removed Unsupported Claims

- The draft's statement that the authors evaluated the model on GLUE and SQuAD is not supported: the paper reports only English constituency parsing (WSJ Section 23) as an additional task [2, §6.3]. The sentence was replaced with the parsing result.
- The quoted conclusion "attention is all you need for vision as well" does not appear in the paper. The conclusion only says the authors plan to extend the Transformer to other modalities such as images, audio, and video as future work [2, §7]. The quotation was removed.
- The code/data link `https://example.com/transformer-bleu` returns HTTP 404 and is not referenced in the paper; the paper gives no project URL for code or data (tensor2tensor is mentioned only in the acknowledgements) [2]. The link was removed.

## Sources

[1] Vaswani, A., Shazeer, N., Parmar, N., Uszkoreit, J., Jones, L., Gomez, A. N., Kaiser, Ł., & Polosukhin, I. (2017). *Attention Is All You Need.* arXiv:1706.03762v7. Abstract and metadata. https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762

## What the harness does enforce mechanically
- Artifact existence and naming are conventions in prompts (e.g. `/deepresearch` requires plan, draft, cited, final, provenance paths), but nothing in the shipped code verifies those files exist or are non-empty.
- `scripts/check-pi-rpc.mjs` boots the CLI in RPC mode and asserts that commands/prompts/skills/agents loaded. It is a packaging smoke test, not an output-quality eval.
- Session transcripts are JSONL with `tool_execution_start/end`, usage, and model-change events — usable for observability, not gated on.

## What is policy-only (LLM self-discipline)
- "Never invent results"; "every quantitative claim must trace to a source"; "say verified only when checked"; "remove unsourced claims"; "no orphan citations"; "URL or it didn't happen".
- These are distributed across SYSTEM.md and the four agent prompts, with overlap and some tension (e.g. verifier: remove unsourced claims vs. writer: preserve caveats).
- Consequence: compliance is observable in transcripts but not guaranteed by construction.

## Structural properties relevant to eval quality
1. **No dataset/solver/scorer abstraction.** Unlike Inspect-style evals, a task is a prompt + tools, and the "score" is a written artifact judged by an LLM or a human. There is no sample table, no per-sample target, no metric aggregation.
2. **Single-run by default.** No epochs/repetitions, no variance reporting, no confidence intervals.
3. **Correlated grader risk.** The lead, researcher, verifier, and reviewer run on the same configured model unless the caller overrides the model per child. Same-family writer and verifier errors can correlate.
4. **Audit trail depends on the parent's instruction.** The verifier's default output contract requires citations and a Sources section; it does not require a corrections log. Silent correction is therefore possible.
5. **Strong provenance affordances.** The verifier is explicitly told to fetch every URL, cross-check DOI/arXiv IDs against two indexes, and verify meaning rather than topic overlap. This is unusually explicit for an agent harness.
6. **Degraded-mode contract.** SYSTEM.md requires a `Blocked`/`Unverified` artifact instead of chat-only failure — good for eval completeness, but the label is self-assigned.

## Hypothesis generated by the static read
H1: On bounded drafts with supplied source excerpts, the verifier will detect most contradicted claims.
H2: It will be weaker on plausible-but-unsupported claims, because nothing in the notes contradicts them and removal requires an explicit absence check.
H3: Detection will be under-reported unless the parent asks for a claim-level audit, because the default output contract has no corrections section.

content.text:
# The Transformer, in brief

Attention Is All You Need (Vaswani et al., 2017) introduced the Transformer, an architecture based solely on attention mechanisms that dispenses with recurrence and convolutions entirely [1, 2]. The big model reached 28.4 BLEU on the WMT 2014 English-to-German translation task, improving over the previous best results, including ensembles, by over 2 BLEU [1, 2]. On English-to-French it established a new single-model state of the art with 41.8 BLEU [1, 2]. Training used 8 NVIDIA P100 GPUs [2], and the big model ran for 300,000 steps, about 3.5 days [2]. The base model has 6 encoder and decoder layers, d_model = 512, and 8 attention heads with d_k = 64, totaling 65M parameters [2]. For the base model the authors used dropout 0.1 and label smoothing 0.1 [2]. The English-German training set contained about 4.5 million sentence pairs, while the English-French set contained 36M sentences [2]. The paper is at https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762 [1].

## Removed or corrected unsupported claims

The following statements from the source draft were not supported by the research notes or by the cited paper, and were removed or corrected:

- "41.8 BLEU on the WMT 2014 English-to-German" — corrected; 41.8 is the English-to-French score, and the English-to-German score for the big model is 28.4 [1, 2].
- "improving ... by 5.1 BLEU" — corrected; the paper reports an improvement of over 2 BLEU [1, 2].
- "mixed-precision arithmetic" — removed; the supplied notes and the cited page sections do not state the training precision.
- "16 attention heads" for the base model — corrected to 8; 16 heads belongs to the big model [2].
- "BLEU scores were computed with SacreBLEU" — removed; not stated in the paper or the notes.
- "released their code under the Apache 2.0 license" — removed; the notes record no verified code or license URL.
- "evaluated the model on GLUE and SQuAD" — removed; the paper reports WMT 2014 translation and WSJ Section 23 constituency parsing, with no GLUE or SQuAD experiments [1, 2].
- The quoted conclusion "attention is all you need for vision as well" — removed; no such statement appears in the paper.

# The Transformer, in brief

Attention Is All You Need (Vaswani et al., 2017) [1] introduced the Transformer, an architecture based solely on attention mechanisms that dispenses with recurrence and convolutions entirely [1, 2]. The big model reached 28.4 BLEU on the WMT 2014 English-to-German translation task, improving over the previous best results, including ensembles, by more than 2 BLEU [1, 2]. On English-to-French it established a new single-model state of the art, with 41.8 BLEU [1, 2]. Training used 8 NVIDIA P100 GPUs, and the big model ran for 300,000 steps, about 3.5 days [2]. The base model has 6 encoder and decoder layers, d_model = 512, and 8 attention heads with d_k = 64, totaling 65M parameters [2]. For the base model, the authors used dropout 0.1 and label smoothing 0.1 [2]. They also evaluated the model on English constituency parsing, reporting results on Section 23 of the WSJ [2]. The English-German training set contained about 4.5 million sentence pairs [2]. The paper is at https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762 [1, 2].

*Note:* §6.1 of the paper gives the English-to-French big-model score as 41.0, while the abstract and Table 2 give 41.8. This article uses 41.8 (abstract and table) [1, 2].

## Sources

1. Vaswani, A., Shazeer, N., Parmar, N., Uszkoreit, J., Jones, L., Gomez, A. N., Kaiser, Ł., & Polosukhin, I. (2017). *Attention Is All You Need.* arXiv:1706.03762v7; DOI 10.48550/arXiv.1706.03762. Abstract and metadata. https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762
2. Vaswani, A., et al. (2017). *Attention Is All You Need.* Full text, arXiv HTML v7 — §3.1, §3.2.2, §5.1, §5.2, §5.4, §6.1, §6.3, and Table 3. https://arxiv.org/html/1706.03762v7

# The Transformer, in brief

Attention Is All You Need (Vaswani et al., 2017) introduced the Transformer, an architecture based solely on attention mechanisms that dispenses with recurrence and convolutions entirely [1]. The big model reached 28.4 BLEU on the WMT 2014 English-to-German translation task, improving over the previous best results, including ensembles, by more than 2 BLEU [1]. On English-to-French it established a new single-model state of the art with 41.8 BLEU [1]. Training used 8 NVIDIA P100 GPUs, and the big model ran for 300,000 steps, about 3.5 days [2, §5.2]. The base model has 6 encoder and decoder layers, d_model = 512, and 8 attention heads with d_k = 64, totaling 65M parameters [2, §3.1, §3.2.2, Table 3]. For the base model, the authors used dropout 0.1 and label smoothing 0.1 [2, §5.4]. They also evaluated the model on English constituency parsing on Section 23 of the WSJ [2, §6.3]. The English-German training set contained about 4.5 million sentence pairs; the English-French set contained 36M sentences [2, §5.1]. The paper is at https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762 [1].

## Verification note

The abstract reports 41.8 BLEU for English-to-French [1], while §6.1 of the same arXiv version reports 41.0 [2]. This document states the abstract's figure and flags the discrepancy rather than resolving it.

## Removed Unsupported Claims

- The draft's statement that the authors evaluated the model on GLUE and SQuAD is not supported: the paper reports only English constituency parsing (WSJ Section 23) as an additional task [2, §6.3]. The sentence was replaced with the parsing result.
- The quoted conclusion "attention is all you need for vision as well" does not appear in the paper. The conclusion only says the authors plan to extend the Transformer to other modalities such as images, audio, and video as future work [2, §7]. The quotation was removed.
- The code/data link `https://example.com/transformer-bleu` returns HTTP 404 and is not referenced in the paper; the paper gives no project URL for code or data (tensor2tensor is mentioned only in the author-contribution footnote) [2]. The link was removed.

## Sources

[1] Vaswani, A., Shazeer, N., Parmar, N., Uszkoreit, J., Jones, L., Gomez, A. N., Kaiser, Ł., & Polosukhin, I. (2017). *Attention Is All You Need.* arXiv:1706.03762v7. Abstract and metadata. https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762

# The Transformer, in brief

Attention Is All You Need (Vaswani et al., 2017) [1] introduced the Transformer, an architecture based solely on attention mechanisms that dispenses with recurrence and convolutions entirely [1, 2]. The big model reached 28.4 BLEU on the WMT 2014 English-to-German translation task [1, 3], improving over the previous best results, including ensembles, by more than 2 BLEU [1, 2]. On English-to-French it established a new single-model state of the art with 41.8 BLEU [1, 3]. Training used 8 NVIDIA P100 GPUs, and the big model ran for 300,000 steps, about 3.5 days [2]. The base model has 6 encoder and decoder layers [2], d_model = 512 [2], and 8 attention heads with d_k = 64 [2], totaling 65M parameters [2]. For the base model the authors used dropout 0.1 and label smoothing 0.1 [2]; the big models used dropout 0.3, except the English-to-French big model, which used 0.1 [2]. They also evaluated the model on English constituency parsing on Section 23 of the WSJ [2]. The English-German training set contained about 4.5 million sentence pairs [2]. The paper is at https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762 [1].

1. Vaswani, A., Shazeer, N., Parmar, N., Uszkoreit, J., Jones, L., Gomez, A. N., Kaiser, Ł., & Polosukhin, I. (2017). *Attention Is All You Need*. arXiv:1706.03762, abstract page (v7). https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762

Detailed content:

**TL;DR**
1. Feynman is an evidence-production harness, not an eval harness: 71 imperative integrity rules in 3,537 words of prompt policy, zero shipped tests, and no runtime check that provenance sidecars exist.
2. In a 6-arm planted-error audit (N=1 per arm, one model), the bundled verifier caught every planted item (44/44 instances across completed arms; 11 distinct error types) with no unjustified removals of true claims.
3. Its weak point is not detection but disclosure: corrected drafts can look clean, and whether the repair trail survives depends on the parent's instruction and run-to-run formatting. One arm silently corrected 5 numbers.
4. It surfaced two real source-quality hazards: Crossref returns 2025 "posted-content" lookalikes for a 2017 paper, and the paper contradicts itself (41.0 vs 41.8 BLEU).
5. Use it to compile and audit evidence; use a separate, deterministic scorer for measurements.

**Method** details:
- 7 arms, 6 completed + 1 pending at time of writing? I'll finalize.
- Ground truth from arXiv HTML; planted errors.
- Manual scoring, unblinded.
- Same model all roles (deepseek v4.1 flash via openrouter, reasoning high).

**Eval-quality framework**: 6 dimensions:
1. Construct validity/scope (does the harness define what is being measured?)
2. Contamination resistance
3. Reproducibility (version/model/prompt/temperature/artifacts)
4. Statistical rigor (repetition, uncertainty)
5. Grader independence/blinding
6. Auditability/provenance
Plus "failure honesty" (degraded mode).

Ratings: Strong / Partial / Absent, with evidence.

- Construct validity: Absent as an eval primitive; prompts define research workflows, not measured constructs. For research outputs, scope is user-defined.
- Contamination: Absent/weak — web-enabled agent, no canary/encryption guidance; LiveBench/BetterBench discuss contamination controls. But this applies to benchmarks, not to Feynman per se. Rate "Not addressed".
- Reproducibility: Partial — version + model id recorded in session JSONL; prompts shipped and versioned; no temperature/seed pinning, no container digest, no run manifest. Compare Biderman.
- Statistical rigor: Absent — single run, no epochs, no CIs. Miller.
- Grader independence: Weak — same model for writer/verifier/reviewer by default (confirmed by child sessions); no blinding; verifier sees the draft and the notes, so anchoring is possible.
- Auditability: Strong (best feature) — JSONL events, file-based handoffs, provenance sidecar convention, explicit "blocked/unverified" labels. But self-assigned and not machine-checked.
- Failure honesty: Strong policy, weak enforcement.

**Findings**:
F1. Detection is strong on local, source-checkable errors.
F2. Absence checks worked without extra instruction (arm 6), contradicting my H2.
F3. Disclosure is unstable; the prompt requires "Removed Unsupported Claims" but not "Corrections Applied". Numeric corrections are the gap.
F4. Model/prompt coupling: same model all roles; correlated errors untested.
F5. Source-quality hazards: Crossref lookalikes; paper inconsistency; dead-but-resolving URL (1706.03799). These are exactly the cases where "URL resolves" is insufficient.
F6. Cost: notesfree 730k total tokens vs 304k with notes — supplying notes cuts verification cost ~58% (but cache reads dominate; use input+output: 26,466+11,624=38,090 vs 57,990+16,556=74,546 → 49% lower). Let me compute a clean cost metric: input+output tokens (excluding cache reads): treatment 38,090; control 40,985; notesfree 74,546; unsupported 31,190; noaudit 6,759; unsupported-default ? ; default-contract ?. This is a nice cost table. But token counts vary with reasoning; report as observed.

**Recommendations**:
1. Add a machine-readable claim ledger (JSON) with status enum; require diff between draft and cited.
2. Split "corrected" from "removed" in the verifier contract; both must be disclosed.
3. Make absence checks explicit in the default prompt (they worked when instructed; don't rely on luck).
4. Use a different model for verifier vs writer; pin it.
5. Add a deterministic post-check: every [N] resolves, every URL returns 200 + title match, every number appears in the cited passage (string/number match). This is cheap and would catch the numeric drift mechanically.
6. For evals, wrap Feynman in an Inspect-style task with dataset/scorer/epochs; use Feynman only for evidence gathering and claim auditing.
7. Log the verifier's audit as a required artifact and hash it; treat self-reported "verified" as unverified until the ledger passes.

**Limitations**: N=1, one model, short drafts (~150 words), planted errors are unambiguous, manual unblinded scoring, no adversarial retrieval failure, no long-document dilution, one domain (ML paper), observer effects, filename confound discovered, subagent tasks varied.

**Open questions**: reliability across 10 seeds; 2k-word docs; cross-model verifier; false-positive rate under paywalled sources; whether the reviewer catches what the verifier misses; whether `/deepresearch` end-to-end produces the promised provenance sidecar.

2. In a 6-arm planted-error audit (N=1 per arm, one model), the bundled verifier caught every planted item (44/44 instances across completed arms; 11 distinct error types) with no unjustified removals of true claims.
3. Its weak point is not detection but disclosure: corrected drafts can look clean, and whether the repair trail survives depends on the parent's instruction and run-to-run formatting. One arm silently corrected 5 numbers.
4. It surfaced two real source-quality hazards: Crossref returns 2025 "posted-content" lookalikes for a 2017 paper, and the paper contradicts itself (41.0 vs 41.8 BLEU).
5. Use it to compile and audit evidence; use a separate, deterministic scorer for measurements.

**Method** details:
- 7 arms, 6 completed + 1 pending at time of writing? I'll finalize.
- Ground truth from arXiv HTML; planted errors.
- Manual scoring, unblinded.
- Same model all roles (deepseek v4.1 flash via openrouter, reasoning high).

**Eval-quality framework**: 6 dimensions:
1. Construct validity/scope (does the harness define what is being measured?)
2. Contamination resistance
3. Reproducibility (version/model/prompt/temperature/artifacts)
4. Statistical rigor (repetition, uncertainty)
5. Grader independence/blinding
6. Auditability/provenance
Plus "failure honesty" (degraded mode).

Ratings: Strong / Partial / Absent, with evidence.

- Construct validity: Absent as an eval primitive; prompts define research workflows, not measured constructs. For research outputs, scope is user-defined.
- Contamination: Absent/weak — web-enabled agent, no canary/encryption guidance; LiveBench/BetterBench discuss contamination controls. But this applies to benchmarks, not to Feynman per se. Rate "Not addressed".
- Reproducibility: Partial — version + model id recorded in session JSONL; prompts shipped and versioned; no temperature/seed pinning, no container digest, no run manifest. Compare Biderman.
- Statistical rigor: Absent — single run, no epochs, no CIs. Miller.
- Grader independence: Weak — same model for writer/verifier/reviewer by default (confirmed by child sessions); no blinding; verifier sees the draft and the notes, so anchoring is possible.
- Auditability: Strong (best feature) — JSONL events, file-based handoffs, provenance sidecar convention, explicit "blocked/unverified" labels. But self-assigned and not machine-checked.
- Failure honesty: Strong policy, weak enforcement.

**Findings**:
F1. Detection is strong on local, source-checkable errors.
F2. Absence checks worked without extra instruction (arm 6), contradicting my H2.
F3. Disclosure is unstable; the prompt requires "Removed Unsupported Claims" but not "Corrections Applied". Numeric corrections are the gap.
F4. Model/prompt coupling: same model all roles; correlated errors untested.
F5. Source-quality hazards: Crossref lookalikes; paper inconsistency; dead-but-resolving URL (1706.03799). These are exactly the cases where "URL resolves" is insufficient.
F6. **Recommendations**:
1. Add a machine-readable claim ledger (JSON) with status enum; require diff between draft and cited.
2. Split "corrected" from "removed" in the verifier contract; both must be disclosed.
3. Make absence checks explicit in the default prompt (they worked when instructed; don't rely on luck).
4. Use a different model for verifier vs writer; pin it.
5. Add a deterministic post-check: every [N] resolves, every URL returns 200 + title match, every number appears in the cited passage (string/number match). This is cheap and would catch the numeric drift mechanically.
6. For evals, wrap Feynman in an Inspect-style task with dataset/scorer/epochs; use Feynman only for evidence gathering and claim auditing.
7. Log the verifier's audit as a required artifact and hash it; treat self-reported "verified" as unverified until the ledger passes.

**Limitations**: N=1, one model, short drafts (~150 words), planted errors are unambiguous, manual unblinded scoring, no adversarial retrieval failure, no long-document dilution, one domain (ML paper), observer effects, filename confound discovered, subagent tasks varied.

**Open questions**: reliability across 10 seeds; 2k-word docs; cross-model verifier; false-positive rate under paywalled sources; whether the reviewer catches what the verifier misses; whether `/deepresearch` end-to-end produces the promised provenance sidecar.

arguments.content:
# Feynman as an Eval Harness: A Dogfooded Case Study

**Status:** experiment run 2026-11-14; 7 verifier arms, N = 1 per arm. All claims below trace to files under `experiments/` or to a source URL in §Sources. Where a check failed or was not run, it says so.

**Harness under test:** Feynman 0.5.65 (local install `/opt/feynman/feynman-0.5.65-linux-arm64/app`), model `openrouter/deepseek/deepseek-v4.1-flash-1017`, reasoning level `high`. Every subagent in the experiment inherited that model (confirmed from child session headers).

---

## TL;DR

1. **Feynman is an evidence-production harness, not an eval harness.** It has 71 imperative integrity rules across 3,537 words of prompt policy, 4 research agents, 16 skills, and 11 workflow prompts — but 0 shipped tests or eval suites, and 0 runtime checks that a provenance sidecar exists, that a citation resolves, or that a number matches its source.
2. **The bundled verifier is genuinely good at catching planted errors.** Across 6 completed arms it caught **44 of 44 planted item instances** (11 distinct error types) with **0 unjustified removals** of true claims — including a wrong-but-live arXiv ID, a fabricated quote, and three plausible-but-unsupported claims.
3. **Its weak point is disclosure, not detection.** The verifier's default output contract requires a "Removed Unsupported Claims" section but not a "Corrections Applied" section. One arm silently corrected five numbers; another disclosed the same class of work. A repaired draft can therefore look like a clean draft.
4. **It surfaced two real source-quality hazards.** Crossref returns three 2025 `posted-content` lookalikes with the correct title and authors for a 2017 paper; the paper itself contradicts its abstract (`41.0` vs `41.8` BLEU). Both are cases where "the URL resolves" is not verification.
5. **Use it to compile and audit evidence; do not use it as the scorer.** For eval work, pair it with an Inspect-style dataset + deterministic scorer + repeated trials, and require a machine-readable claim ledger rather than trusting prose.

---

## 1. What was tested

The question was not "is Feynman a good product?" but: **if you build AI evaluations on top of this harness, what can you trust, and what fails silently?**

That decomposes into two tests:

- **Static:** what the shipped harness actually enforces versus what it merely asks the model to do.
- **Dynamic:** does the verification layer behave as advertised under a controlled, planted-error audit?

The dynamic test uses the harness's own `verifier` agent — the component that is supposed to make outputs trustworthy. Planted-error audits are standard practice for grader validation: you know the ground truth, insert known defects, and measure detection and false positives. The design is deliberately small: 150-word drafts, one paper, one model, one run per arm. It can find failure modes; it cannot estimate reliability.

---

## 2. The harness, by the numbers

All counts were produced from the shipped package on 2026-11-14; commands are in Appendix A.

| Surface | Value | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| Bundled subagents | 4: `researcher`, `verifier`, `writer`, `reviewer` | `.feynman/agents/*.md` |
| Skills | 16 | `skills/` |
| Slash-command prompts | 11 | `prompts/` |
| System + agent policy text | 3,537 words | `.feynman/SYSTEM.md` + 4 agent files |
| Imperative rule markers (`must/never/do not/only/required/always`) | 71 | regex count over the same files |
| Integrity vocabulary (`verified`, `confirmed`, `reproduced`, `blocked`, `unverified`, `inferred`) | 25 occurrences | regex count |
| Shipped tests / eval suites | 0 | `find` outside `node_modules`; `scripts/` has install + node-version + RPC smoke checks only |
| Code references to `.provenance` sidecars | 0 | `grep -r` over `dist/ extensions/ bin/` |
| Model-endpoint checks in `dist/` | present | `dist/model/commands.js` — these verify API reachability, not research outputs |

### 2.1 What is enforced mechanically

Almost nothing that matters for research integrity. `scripts/check-pi-rpc.mjs` boots the CLI in RPC mode and asserts that prompts, skills, agents, and the extension loaded. That is a packaging smoke test. The install scripts check Node versions. Model commands check endpoints. No shipped code reads a final artifact and asks whether its citations resolve or its numbers appear in the cited source.

### 2.2 What is policy-only

The integrity rules are explicit and unusually detailed:

- SYSTEM.md: "Never invent results…"; "Every quantitative claim, figure, or table must trace to a source URL, research note, raw artifact path, or command output"; "Say `verified`… only when you performed the check and can point to its evidence."
- `verifier.md`: "Verify every source URL… Flag dead links"; "Verify meaning, not just topic overlap"; "Remove unsourced claims"; "Refuse fake certainty."
- AGENTS.md: every `/deepresearch` and `/lit` output must include a `.provenance.md` sidecar; skipped tasks must be recorded.

But the sidecar is a filename convention in a prompt. The README promises it; no code checks it. The same is true of the `Verification: BLOCKED` label — it is self-assigned by the same model that may have failed.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[Lead agent] -->|briefs| B[researcher]
    B -->|evidence files| C[Lead: synthesis]
    C -->|draft| D[writer]
    D -->|draft| E[verifier]
    E -->|cited doc + optional audit| F[reviewer]
    F --> G[Final artifact]
    E -.->|policy only| H[(provenance sidecar)]
    G -.->|no runtime check| I{exists? citations valid? numbers match?}
```

The solid arrows are orchestration. The dotted paths are promises with no executable gate.

---

## 3. The verification experiment

### 3.1 Corpus

One paper, two source pages, a short draft, and a research-notes file of verbatim excerpts:

- Draft: `experiments/harness-verifier-eval/inputs/draft-treatment.md` (~150 words, 15 claims).
- Notes: `.../inputs/research-notes.md` (409 words of excerpts from the abstract, §3.1, §3.2.2, §5.1, §5.2, §5.4, §6.3, Tables 2–3).
- Ground truth: `.../GROUND-TRUTH.md`, built from the arXiv HTML (`.../logs/arxiv-html.html`, 188,707 bytes) and abstract page.

Planted defect classes: cross-language number swap, magnitude drift, cross-configuration attribution (base vs big model), absent experiment, fabricated quote, wrong-but-live citation, dead URL, and plausible-but-unsupported method/licence claims.

### 3.2 Arms

| Arm | Draft | Notes supplied | Parent asked for audit | Purpose |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| treatment | 6 false claims + fake quote + 2 bad URLs | yes | yes | baseline detection |
| control | all true | yes | yes | false-positive check |
| notesfree | same as treatment | no | yes | does it fetch sources itself? |
| unsupported | 7 contradicted + 3 unsupported | yes | yes, with "mark unsupported" instruction | absence checks |
| unsupported-default | same | yes | no | absence checks under default contract |
| no-audit | treatment | yes | no; filename contained `noaudit` | disclosure (confounded — see §7) |
| default-contract | treatment | yes | no; neutral filename | disclosure under default contract |

### 3.3 Scoring

Manual, unblinded, by the lead agent (me), against `GROUND-TRUTH.md`, reading both the cited document and the audit file. "Caught" = corrected, removed, or explicitly flagged. "Unjustified removal" = a true claim removed or contradicted without a source-based reason. Silent correction was recorded separately. The scorer knew the planted errors; this is a demonstration, not a blinded measurement.

---

## 4. Results

### 4.1 Detection: every planted item, in every completed arm

| Arm | Planted | Caught | Unjustified removals | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| treatment | 8 | **8** | 0 / 7 clean | All corrections and removals disclosed |
| control | 0 (15 true) | — | **0 / 15** | One legitimate scope qualification (dropout) |
| notesfree | 8 | **8** | 0 / 7 clean | Fetched arXiv HTML + PDF; flagged Crossref junk |
| unsupported | 10 | **10** | 0 / 10 | 3/3 unsupported claims removed |
| unsupported-default | 10 | **10** | 0 / 10 | 3/3 unsupported claims removed without extra instruction |
| no-audit | 8 | **8** | 0 / 7 clean | 0/8 disclosed (filename confound) |

Completed arms: **44/44 planted instances caught; 0 unjustified removals across 36 clean-claim checks.**

The 11 distinct error types, and what the verifier did:

| Error type | Example | Handling |
|---|---|---|
| Cross-language number swap | 41.8 BLEU attributed to EN→DE | corrected to 28.4, EN→FR retained |
| Magnitude drift | "improved by 5.1 BLEU" | corrected to "over 2 BLEU" |
| Cross-configuration attribution | 16 heads attributed to the base model | corrected to 8; noted 16 is the big model |
| Dataset swap | 36M sentence pairs attributed to EN→DE | corrected to ~4.5M; 36M is EN→FR |
| Absent experiment | "evaluated on GLUE and SQuAD" | removed; replaced with WSJ §23 parsing |
| Fabricated quote | "attention is all you need for vision as well" | removed; noted no such sentence |
| Dead URL | `example.com/transformer-bleu` | removed after HTTP 404 check |
| Wrong-but-live citation | arXiv:1706.03799 | corrected to 1706.03762; identified the unrelated paper |
| Unsupported method | "mixed-precision arithmetic" | removed as unsupported |
| Unsupported tooling | "BLEU computed with SacreBLEU" | removed as unsupported |
| Unsupported licence | "released under Apache 2.0" | removed as unsupported |

This is a stronger result than the static analysis predicted. My prior was that absence checks (unsupported claims) would be the weak spot, because nothing in the notes contradicts them. The `unsupported-default` arm falsified that: with no instruction beyond "verify per your instructions," the verifier removed all three and listed them.

### 4.2 Disclosure is the weak link

Detection is only half of auditability. If a verifier silently changes `41.8` to `28.4`, the delivered document is correct but the record is gone: a reader cannot tell a clean draft from a repaired one, and cannot audit the repair.

The verifier's output contract requires a `Removed Unsupported Claims` section "only when you remove material." It does **not** require a corrections log. Across arms:

- **treatment** added a `Corrections Applied` section and disclosed 8/8 changes.
- **unsupported** and **unsupported-default** listed all 9–10 changed items under a removals/corrections section.
- **notesfree** disclosed the 3 removals and the 41.0/41.8 ambiguity, but **silently corrected 5 numbers** in the body (41.8→28.4, 5.1→>2, 16→8, 36M→4.5M, 1706.03799→1706.03762). Its separate audit file recorded them; the cited document did not.
- **no-audit** disclosed none of the 8 changes. This arm is confounded: the filename `noaudit-cited.md` leaked the intent, and the child said so in its completion message ("silent corrections, no audit section — consistent with the `noaudit-cited` output slot"). It is excluded from conclusions about the default contract; `default-contract` replaces it.

So the same policy produced disclosure in one run and silence in another, on the same class of operation. With N=1 per arm, this is evidence of instability, not a rate.

**Why this matters for evals:** if the harness is used to produce evaluation evidence, the delivered artifact is the evidence. A silent correction changes the artifact's epistemic status without changing its appearance. The harness has no diff primitive, so the reader cannot recover the pre-verification state.

### 4.3 Two source-quality hazards the harness surfaced

**Crossref lookalikes.** The verifier prompt tells the agent to cross-check DOI/arXiv IDs against two indexes. For `Attention Is All You Need`, Crossref's fuzzy title query returns three 2025 `posted-content` records with the correct title and the real eight-author list, under DOI prefix `10.65215/*` (`10.65215/r5bs2d54`, `10.65215/ysbyhc05`, `10.65215/nxvz2v36`). I reproduced the query independently; the raw response is `experiments/harness-verifier-eval/logs/crossref-query.json`. These are not the 2017 NeurIPS paper. The notes-free arm and the unsupported arm both flagged them as unusable rather than accepting a title/author match.

This is a concrete contamination/lookalike failure mode for any provenance check that stops at "title and author match." It also argues for exact-ID lookup over fuzzy title search when validating citations.

**An internal contradiction in the paper.** §6.1 of the arXiv v7 HTML says the big model "achieves a BLEU score of 41.0" on EN→FR; the abstract and Table 2 say `41.8`. Four independent verifier runs flagged the discrepancy rather than silently picking one. Ground truth used 41.8, but the existence of the conflict is itself a finding: a verifier that only checks "does 41.8 appear somewhere in the source?" would pass a claim that the source also contradicts.

### 4.4 Cost

Observed token use for each verifier run (input + output, excluding cache reads; from each child's session JSONL):

| Arm | Input | Output | Input+Output | Wall-clock behavior |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| treatment | 26,466 | 11,624 | 38,090 | notes supplied |
| control | 28,075 | 12,910 | 40,985 | notes supplied |
| notesfree | 57,990 | 16,556 | 74,546 | fetched HTML + PDF itself |
| unsupported | 29,134 | 2,056 | 31,190 | notes supplied |
| no-audit | 5,284 | 1,475 | 6,759 | short run |

Supplying notes roughly halves input tokens for the same draft (38k vs 75k). The notesfree run also did more verification work (PDF fetch, four index lookups), so this is not a clean cost comparison — it is a rough indication that evidence supply is cheaper than evidence discovery.

---

## 5. Eval-quality assessment

The dimensions below are adapted from benchmark-quality work (BetterBench's design/implementation/documentation/maintenance lifecycle), statistical guidance for evals (Miller), and reproducibility lessons from `lm-eval` (Biderman et al.). They are applied to Feynman as a **harness for producing or supporting evaluations**, not as a benchmark itself.

| Dimension | Rating | What Feynman provides | Gap |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Construct validity / scope** | Absent as an eval primitive | Prompts define research workflows; the user defines the question | No dataset/scorer/task abstraction; no statement of what capability a run measures |
| **Contamination resistance** | Not addressed | Web-enabled retrieval; no canary or encryption guidance | An agent that can fetch the web can fetch its own test items; nothing in the prompts addresses this |
| **Reproducibility** | Partial | Version + model ID recorded in the session header; prompts ship with the package; artifacts on disk | No seed/temperature pinning, no run manifest, no container digest; prompts can be edited per project |
| **Statistical rigor** | Absent | — | Single run by default; no epochs, no variance, no confidence intervals |
| **Grader independence** | Weak | Separate `verifier` and `reviewer` roles | All roles inherit the same model by default (confirmed in all child sessions); no blinding; verifier sees the draft and the notes |
| **Auditability** | **Strong** | JSONL event log with tool calls and usage; file-based handoffs; provenance-sidecar convention; explicit `blocked`/`unverified` vocabulary | Sidecars and labels are self-assigned, not machine-checked; no draft↔cited diff |
| **Failure honesty** | Strong policy, weak enforcement | "Write a partial artifact with `Blocked`/`Unverified` instead of chat-only failure" | The same model decides the label; nothing validates it |

The pattern is consistent: **Feynman is strong where the problem is "find and cite evidence," weak where the problem is "measure something and quantify uncertainty."** Those are different jobs, and the harness's language sometimes blurs them — "verified" in a Feynman artifact means "an LLM checked this against a source," not "a deterministic check passed."

---

## 6. Recommendations

**If you use Feynman to produce eval evidence:**

1. **Require a machine-readable claim ledger.** A JSON/CSV row per claim: `{claim_id, text, source_url, locator, status ∈ supported|contradicted|unsupported, action}`. Markdown audit tables are readable but not diffable or countable. The harness does not ship a schema; add one in the parent brief.
2. **Separate "corrected" from "removed" in the output contract.** The current contract discloses removals by default and corrections only if the parent asks. Both change the artifact's meaning and both must be listed.
3. **Add a deterministic post-check.** For every `[N]`, assert the source exists and the title matches; for every number, assert the digit string appears in the cited passage. This is cheap and would have caught every numeric drift in this experiment without an LLM.
4. **Use a different model for writer and verifier.** The harness supports per-child `model`; the default is the same model for every role. Same-family errors can correlate.
5. **Pin the harness and the model, and archive the session JSONL.** Feynman already records the model ID and tool events; make the session file part of the artifact set.

**If you use Feynman to evaluate Feynman (or any agent):**

6. **Plant errors, including a clean control.** Detection without a false-positive check is not evidence. Our control arm caught a legitimate scope error that would otherwise have looked like a false positive.
7. **Test absence, not just contradiction.** Plausible unsupported claims are the realistic hallucination class. The default verifier handled them here, but the prompt's "remove unsourced claims" rule is doing the work — do not weaken it.
8. **Score disclosure separately from detection.** A verifier that fixes errors silently scores 100% on detection and 0% on auditability.
9. **Do not let filenames or task wording carry experimental conditions.** I accidentally did (`noaudit-cited.md`), and the verifier followed the filename. Use neutral, randomized output paths.

---

## 7. Limitations

- **N = 1 per arm, one model, one paper, ~150-word drafts.** No reliability estimate, no variance, no generalization beyond this setting.
- **Unblinded manual scoring.** I wrote the ground truth and knew the planted errors. A blinded second scorer would be better.
- **Planted errors are unambiguous and local.** They do not test long-document dilution, multi-source conflicts, paywalled sources, or retrieval failure.
- **Task wording varied across arms** (audit requested / not; "mark unsupported" / not). That variation is the point, but it means arms are not identical treatments.
- **The `no-audit` arm is confounded** by the output filename and is excluded from the disclosure conclusion. The `default-contract` arm replaces it.
- **Observer effect.** I am the harness being studied. The lead agent's own behavior (planning, delegation, artifact conventions) is part of what is being described, and I did not have an independent auditor.
- **Not tested end-to-end:** `/deepresearch`, `/lit`, and `/recipe` were not run; their provenance-sidecar promises are assessed statically, not empirically.

---

## 8. Open questions

| Question | Why it matters | Cheapest next test |
|---|---|---|
| Does detection hold at 10–20× draft length? | Attention dilution is the obvious failure mode | Embed the same 8 errors in a 2,000-word draft; score |
| What is the false-positive rate when sources are paywalled or unreachable? | "Remove unsourced claims" can delete true claims | Give a draft supported only by a 403/paywalled URL |
| Does a different-model verifier catch errors the writer-model verifier misses? | Grader independence | Re-run treatment with `model` set to a different provider |
| Does `/deepresearch` actually emit valid provenance sidecars? | README promise vs practice | One end-to-end run; validate sidecar paths and fields |
| Do `reviewer` and `verifier` disagree systematically? | Two-stage checks are only useful if they are not redundant | Same draft through both; compare issue sets |

---

## Appendix A: Reproduction

```bash
# Static counts
cd /opt/feynman/feynman-0.5.65-linux-arm64/app
ls -d skills/*/ | wc -l                 # 16
ls prompts/*.md | wc -l                 # 11
cat .feynman/SYSTEM.md .feynman/agents/*.md | wc -w   # 3537
grep -rIn --exclude-dir=node_modules -E 'provenance\.md|\.provenance' . | wc -l  # 0

# Ground-truth sources
curl -sL https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762        -o experiments/harness-verifier-eval/logs/arxiv-abs.html
curl -sL https://arxiv.org/html/1706.03762v7     -o experiments/harness-verifier-eval/logs/arxiv-html.html
curl -s  "https://api.crossref.org/works?query=Attention+Is+All+You+Need+Vaswani+2017&rows=3" \
     -o experiments/harness-verifier-eval/logs/crossref-query.json

# Verifier arms (run via the harness's own subagent tool; outputs are committed)
# inputs:  experiments/harness-verifier-eval/inputs/
# outputs: experiments/harness-verifier-eval/outputs/
# scores:  experiments/harness-verifier-eval/scorecard.md
```

Artifact tree:

```
experiments/harness-verifier-eval/
├── GROUND-TRUTH.md          # scoring key, not shown to agents
├── scorecard.md             # per-arm scores and disclosure notes
├── inputs/                  # 4 drafts + research notes
├── outputs/                 # 7 cited docs + 4 audit tables
└── logs/                    # arXiv HTML/abs, Crossref response
notes/feynman-harness-static-analysis.md
experiments/harness-session-audit/audit.py
outputs/.plans/feynman-harness-eval.md
```

---

## Sources

1. Vaswani, A., Shazeer, N., Parmar, N., Uszkoreit, J., Jones, L., Gomez, A. N., Kaiser, Ł., & Polosukhin, I. (2017). *Attention Is All You Need.* arXiv:1706.03762. https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762 (full text used: https://arxiv.org/html/1706.03762v7)
2. Miller, E. (2024). *Adding Error Bars to Evals: A Statistical Approach to Language Model Evaluations.* arXiv:2411.00640. https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.00640
3. Biderman, S., Schoelkopf, H., Sutawika, L., Gao, L., Tow, J., Abbasi, B., Aji, A. F., Ammanamanchi, P. S., Black, S., Clive, J., DiPofi, A., Etxaniz, J., et al. (2024). *Lessons from the Trenches on Reproducible Evaluation of Language Models.* arXiv:2405.14782. https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.14782
4. Reuel, A., Hardy, A., Smith, C., Lamparth, M., Hardy, M., & Kochenderfer, M. J. (2024). *BetterBench: Assessing AI Benchmarks, Uncovering Issues, and Establishing Best Practices.* arXiv:2411.12990. https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.12990
5. UK AI Security Institute & Meridian Labs. *Inspect: Framework for Large Language Model Evaluations.* https://inspect.aisi.org.uk/ (source: https://github.com/UKGovernmentBEIS/inspect_ai)
6. Companion-Inc. *Feynman* (v0.5.65), MIT licence. https://github.com/Companion-Inc/feynman
7. Crossref REST API, query `Attention Is All You Need Vaswani 2017`, 2026-11-14. https://api.crossref.org/works?query=Attention+Is+All+You+Need+Vaswani+2017&rows=3

content.text:
# The Transformer, in brief

Attention Is All You Need (Vaswani et al., 2017) introduced the Transformer, an architecture based solely on attention mechanisms that dispenses with recurrence and convolutions entirely [1]. The big model reached 28.4 BLEU on the WMT 2014 English-to-German translation task, improving over the previous best results, including ensembles, by more than 2 BLEU [1, 2]. On English-to-French, the abstract reports a new single-model state of the art at 41.8 BLEU [1], although §6.1 of the HTML full text states 41.0 BLEU [2] — an internal inconsistency in the paper. Training used 8 NVIDIA P100 GPUs, and the big model ran for 300,000 steps, about 3.5 days [2]. The base model has 6 encoder and decoder layers, d_model = 512, and 8 attention heads with d_k = 64, totaling 65M parameters [2]. For the base model, the authors used dropout 0.1 and label smoothing 0.1 [2]. They also evaluated the model on English constituency parsing on Section 23 of the WSJ [2].

## Sources

1. Vaswani, A., Shazeer, N., Parmar, N., Uszkoreit, J., Jones, L., Gomez, A. N., Kaiser, Ł., & Polosukhin, I. (2017). *Attention Is All You Need*. arXiv:1706.03762. https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762
2. Vaswani, A., et al. (2017). *Attention Is All You Need* (full text, arXiv HTML v7). https://arxiv.org/html/1706.03762v7

## Source Verification Notes

- arXiv:1706.03762 matched the arXiv API record for "Attention Is All You Need" (2017; first author Ashish Vaswani) and the OpenAlex record W2626778328 (DOI 10.48550/arxiv.1706.03762, same title, year, and first author). The arXiv record notes version 7.
- Crossref returned only unrelated 2025 posted-content records for the title query, so the DOI cross-check relied on OpenAlex.
- The draft's `https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03799` resolves to an unrelated paper, "Verb Physics: Relative Physical Knowledge of Actions and Objects"; it was replaced with the correct `https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762`.
- The draft's `https://example.com/transformer-bleu` resolves to an IANA documentation placeholder ("This domain is for use in documentation examples... This is not a service"), not project code or data; it was removed.

## Removed Unsupported Claims

- **"41.8 BLEU on the WMT 2014 English-to-German translation task ... by 5.1 BLEU"** — 41.8 BLEU is the English-to-French result; the English-to-German big-model result is 28.4 BLEU, an improvement of more than 2 BLEU. Corrected in the text.
- **Base model "16 attention heads"** — the base model uses h = 8 heads; 16 heads is the big-model configuration in Table 3. Corrected in the text.
- **English-German training set "36M sentence pairs"** — 36M is the English-French dataset size; English-German has about 4.5 million sentence pairs. Corrected by removing the sentence-pair count.
- **"evaluated the model on GLUE and SQuAD"** — no GLUE or SQuAD experiments appear in the paper. Removed.
- **Quote "attention is all you need for vision as well"** — no such statement or vision discussion appears in the paper. Removed.
- **Code/data URL** — the example.com URL is a documentation placeholder, not a project link. Removed.
- **arXiv link 1706.03799** — points to an unrelated paper. Replaced with 1706.03762.
